A field report from an artificial economy

Bitcoin vs. the Printing Press

The agents in Barry Becker’s economy simulator now act more like real people. Employers renegotiate pay when prices fall, and central banks print when a crisis hits. We put the new version to work on five questions about money and the average household.

“Bitcoin”: a fixed money supply “Fiat”: central-bank money that grows “Hybrid”: fixed money with a lender of last resort
Based on Barry Becker’s agent-based simulator · experiments and write-up by an AI analyst · October 2026

A small economy you can rerun at will

Barry Becker is a retired software engineer and the author of the novel Into the Singularity. He built an agent-based economy simulator: thousands of simulated households, hundreds of firms, a handful of banks, a government and (under fiat) a central bank. Month by month for twenty simulated years, they work, shop, borrow, save, renegotiate wages and sometimes go bust. Nobody tells the economy what to do. Booms, slumps, inflation and deflation all emerge from millions of small decisions.

That makes it a laboratory for a question usually argued in slogans: would ordinary people be better off with bitcoin-like money that can’t be printed, or with ordinary government money? This report uses the simulator as it stands today to ask that question five ways. Each case has a button that opens the live app with the same settings, so you can rerun it yourself.

“The simulation cannot show that one monetary system is better in the real world. It shows which assumptions a conclusion depends on.”

How to read the charts

Each line is the month-by-month median of 10 simulated histories (random seeds 1–10), lightly smoothed. “Typical household’s real consumption” is the median household’s consumption in goods, not dollars or sats, so fiat and bitcoin can be compared directly.

Two kinds of number

  • Runs numbers come from a 10-run experiment on the current simulator: 4,000 households, 200 firms and 4 banks over 240 months (20 years). “Average” means the average over years 2–20. Where two settings are compared, we also say how many of the 10 paired runs agree.
  • Live app buttons open the deployed app with exactly those settings. Press Run to reproduce the charts. We ran nine of these settings in the live app (Chrome) and compared them with our runs. Seven matched digit for digit. Two, “no inherited mortgages” and the gradual transition, drift a little: Chrome’s JavaScript engine and the one we used round some numbers differently, and over 20 simulated years the tiny differences grow. Expect those two to come out close to our figures, not identical. In a 10-run check in Chrome, year-20 unemployment differed from ours by 0.1–0.2 points.
One setting held fixed throughout: AI adoption is set to None, so the results are about money, not robots. The app’s default has AI adoption switched on, which slowly pushes up unemployment over time in every regime. Prices and output respond to demand, households open with today’s mix of renters, owners and mortgages, and random shocks hit about once a decade unless a case says otherwise.
The five cases at a glance
01Same economy, two monies. Bitcoin prices fall about 3.6% a year. Unemployment runs 2.8 points higher, and the typical household consumes 9% less on average. A real slump needs very sticky wages. 02Old debts, falling prices. A mortgage book inherited from the fiat world is what drags bitcoin households down late in the run. Without it, the year-20 gap falls from about 30% to about 13%. 03Pay cuts instead of pink slips. Under bitcoin, money wages fall by almost half over 20 years. The faster pay is renegotiated, the fewer jobs are lost. 04When the printer runs. In a stormy economy, an aggressive printing press buys the lowest unemployment, but prices rise almost sixfold and real wages fall furthest. Bitcoin households keep their purchasing power but lose jobs. 05Two monies at once? The app’s “hybrid” prevents every bank failure. But it can’t yet model households freely choosing which money to hold, and here is what that would take.
01
Case one · The baseline

Same economy, two kinds of money

Start with the simplest experiment. Take one economy and run it twice, once with central-bank money and once with a fixed supply. Nothing else changes. Under fiat, prices rise about 3% a year and roughly double over 20 years. Under bitcoin they fall about 3.6% a year and end at less than half their starting level. Employers respond by cutting money wages, and a worker who keeps a job ends up with slightly more purchasing power than under fiat. But fewer people keep their jobs, and the typical household falls steadily behind.

Live app▶ Fiat baseline▶ Bitcoin baselineTo overlay the two: open the fiat link, press Run, press “Pin as baseline”, switch the Monetary regime to bitcoin and press Run again. Ten runs at full size take a few minutes in a browser; set “Num seeds” to 1 for a quick look.

What would it take to turn deflation into a slump?

Bitcoin’s jobs penalty in the default app is real but moderate. To get a genuine deflationary slump, with unemployment in the teens, you have to change the assumptions about how people behave. We tried three, one at a time and then together. Making debtors three times as sensitive to deflation barely moved average unemployment. Having people expect deflation to continue, instead of anchoring on the regime’s trend, barely moved it either. Very sticky wages (pay closes only 5% of the gap each month instead of 10%) is what does it: unemployment averages 8.5% and peaks at 13.3%. Going the other way, if wages reset at once, unemployment drops to 6.1%.

Live app▶ Very sticky wages▶ All three “stiff” assumptions▶ Fully flexible wages
Flexible wages close the jobs gap, not the living-standards gap. When wages reset instantly in both worlds, bitcoin unemployment is only 0.4 points above fiat’s (6.1% vs 5.9%). The typical household still consumes about 11% less under bitcoin. Something besides lost jobs is at work, and Case 2 finds most of it.
So what

In this economy, gentle deflation costs some jobs, and a deflationary slump needs paychecks that adjust very slowly. The bigger question is who ends up with the wealth.

02
Case two · Who carries the debt

Old debts in a world of falling prices

Every run opens with households as they are today: about two-thirds own their homes, and 62% of those owners carry a mortgage, so about 40% of all households start out owing a fixed sum of money. Under fiat, inflation slowly shrinks that debt. Under bitcoin, falling prices and wages make it heavier every year. Take the inherited mortgages away and the picture changes. Both worlds get richer, but bitcoin gains far more by the end of the run.

Live app▶ Bitcoin, today’s mortgage book▶ Bitcoin, no inherited mortgages▶ Fiat, no inherited mortgagesIn Chrome, the “no inherited mortgages” bitcoin run comes out close to our figures but not digit for digit (see “Two kinds of number”).
Barry’s view

Barry’s view is that a mortgage as we know it, a long loan fixed in money, doesn’t make sense under a bitcoin standard. Nobody would sign one expecting their wages to fall every year. Seen that way, the fairest comparison is a bitcoin world without the inherited book against today’s fiat world with it. On that comparison the typical bitcoin household consumes 4.5% more on average over the 20 years (higher in all 10 runs) and ends year 20 about 4% behind. Unemployment is still 2.7 points higher.

Honest caveats: this setting removes only the opening mortgages. In the debt-free bitcoin world, new home loans still get written (about 97 per run over 20 years among 4,000 households). Banks that start without a mortgage book also fail more often: 16.5 failures by year 20, compared with 5 when they hold the book (fiat: 5.5 vs 3). That looks like a quirk of how bank income is modelled, and it deserves a closer look before anyone leans on it.
So what

Much of bitcoin’s late-run damage comes from debts written for a world of rising prices. Any real transition would have to deal with them first.

03
Case three · How firms adjust

Pay cuts instead of pink slips

In the current simulator, every firm’s pay drifts toward an agreed wage set by the price level, productivity and how tight the job market is. The negotiation is symmetric. When prices rise, workers win raises. When prices fall, employers win pay cuts, at the same speed. A firm whose sales drop can also shed staff, but at most 5% of its workforce a month. So in a deflation, firms have two levers: cut pay or cut jobs. How fast pay can be renegotiated decides which one carries the load.

A twist under fiat: instant renegotiation isn’t free there. Fiat unemployment rises from 4.2% to 5.9% when pay resets at once. In this model, a little stickiness seems to cushion fiat while prices are rising, and to hurt bitcoin while they are falling.
So what

Falling prices don’t have to mean layoffs. In this model, the faster employers and workers can agree on lower pay, the fewer jobs deflation costs.

04
Case four · Crises and the printing press

When the printer runs

The simulator’s fiat central bank now prints when a crisis hits. When unemployment rises more than two points above its natural rate, it speeds up money growth a few months later. It also can’t freeze the money supply: some growth always happens. To test this, we made the world stormy. A new boom-and-bust shock starts as soon as the last one ends, and each is three times the default size. Then we compared four rulebooks: fiat with crisis printing switched off, fiat with it on (the default), a full “printing press” (maximum crisis stimulus, a central bank that buys half of new government debt, and deficit spending), and bitcoin.

How fiat and bitcoin households fare

A fiat household is far more likely to keep its job through the busts. Its cash savings, though, lose 5–7% of their value a year. By year 20 its paycheck buys 5–11% less than a bitcoin paycheck, and under the printing press real pay grows just 4% in 20 years (bitcoin: 18%). The printing press also brings more bank failures (8.5 by year 20, compared with 1 for ordinary fiat). A bitcoin household that keeps its job sees its pay buy a little more each year, and its cash gains value. But at the worst point of a bust about one worker in six is out of work, and wealth piles up at the top. The richest fifth hold 70% of household wealth, compared with 55–56% under fiat, and the poorest fifth hold 2.0% (fiat: 3.3–3.9%).

Barry’s view

Barry doubts that politicians could ever hold money growth at zero. The pull, in a crisis or before an election, is always toward printing more. The current app builds that doubt in. Fiat money growth can’t be set to zero, and crisis stimulus is on by default. He also sees helicopter money as meaningless under bitcoin, and the app agrees: bitcoin and hybrid worlds simply ignore the stimulus and money-growth settings. What the app doesn’t yet model is a central bank whose printing ratchets up over time as political pressure builds. The “printing press” here is a fixed rulebook, not a slide.

So what

Printing trades jobs for prices. In this model, a heavy printing press buys a few points of employment at the cost of a near-sixfold price level and the weakest paycheck. Bitcoin trades the other way.

05
Case five · The hybrid question

Two monies at once?

The most realistic future may not be “all bitcoin” or “all fiat”. It may be a hybrid, where people and firms hold whichever money they trust. We asked how far the current app can take that question. It has three pieces. They’re worth seeing, but none of them is yet an economy where each household chooses its own money.

Piece 1: the “hybrid” regime is bitcoin with a safety net

Choose hybrid and the economy runs on fixed-supply money, like bitcoin, except that the central bank stands by as a lender of last resort. If a bank’s equity goes negative, the central bank injects just enough reserves to keep it alive. That rescue is the only new money ever created. The result: zero bank failures in every run (bitcoin: 5 by year 20), and a typical household that ends year 20 about 22% better off than under plain bitcoin, though still behind fiat. Unemployment is no different from bitcoin’s.

Piece 2: a currency-choice scoreboard

Turn on Money choice speed and the app tracks the shares of fiat, bitcoin, stablecoins and a central-bank digital currency. Each month they drift toward the mix favoured by legal-tender pull, trust, payment friction and real return. At the default trust level, bitcoin’s share climbs from 0.4% to 16% within about two years and its price rises twelvefold. At high trust (1.5) it reaches 36%, level with fiat, and its price hits the model’s 20× ceiling by year 8. The catch: nothing else in the economy changes, not even by a cent. In all 10 runs every series except the money shares and the bitcoin price is identical to the run with choice switched off. For now the shares are a scoreboard, not a choice anyone acts on.

Live app▶ Hybrid regime▶ Fiat + money choice▶ Money choice, high bitcoin trustWith money choice on, open the “Money” chart group to see the shares.

Piece 3: a five-year window when both monies circulate

The closest thing to two currencies side by side is the gradual transition. For five years, a slice of every deposit and every loan is converted into bitcoin each month, and shops accept either balance. Then the economy moves fully onto bitcoin. Here is how that compares with an overnight switch at month 60 and with staying on fiat. During the window itself, nothing much happens. Once bitcoin rules take over, unemployment climbs to 13–14% within five years. Averaged over years 2–20, the gradual route ends slightly worse than the overnight switch: unemployment averages 10.3% vs 9.2%, higher in 9 of 10 runs, and bank failures reach 11 vs 7.

Live app▶ Gradual, both monies for 5 years▶ Overnight switch at month 60In Chrome, the gradual run comes out close to our figures but not digit for digit (see “Two kinds of number”).
Why this isn’t yet the hybrid economy Barry wants to evaluate: in the transition window, conversion is forced. Everyone converts the same slice each month, whether or not they want to. Nobody chooses to hold bitcoin because they distrust the printing press, and nobody holds onto fiat because they owe taxes in it. A true hybrid needs households and firms that each pick a currency mix, prices quoted in both, and a bitcoin price set by that demand. The pieces above are the scaffolding.
So what

A safety net for banks is the single most helpful “hybrid” feature the app can test today. The richer question, who would choose bitcoin and how the average household would fare, needs one more piece of model.

The big picture

The coin matters less than the plumbing around it

Across all five cases, whether fixed-supply money helps or hurts the average household depends on a few features that have little to do with the coin itself:

1How fast pay adjusts

Quick wage renegotiation turns deflation into pay cuts rather than layoffs. Very sticky pay turns it into a slump (Cases 1 and 3).

2What debts people carry

Loans written for a world of rising prices get heavier as prices fall. That inherited book explains much of bitcoin’s late-run damage (Case 2).

3How hard the printer runs

Some printing steadies jobs. A heavy printing press buys a little more employment at the cost of prices and paychecks (Case 4).

4Whether banks have a safety net

A lender of last resort on top of fixed money prevents every bank failure here and leaves households better off than plain bitcoin (Case 5).

What the current app does not do (yet)

No free choice of currency. Households and firms can’t pick their own mix of fiat and bitcoin. The money-choice shares are tracked but don’t change anyone’s behaviour, and the “hybrid” regime is bitcoin money plus a lender of last resort. A world where both monies circulate by choice is the most important missing piece.
One closed economy, one price. There is no foreign trade, and goods have a single price. During a transition, bitcoin balances are converted at one exchange rate, which follows a simple rule capped at 20× its starting value.
Today’s debts in every world. Bitcoin runs open with a 2026-style mortgage book. Removing it helps households but raises bank failures, which suggests bank income needs more realistic modelling.
Printing is a fixed rule. Crisis stimulus responds to unemployment, but nothing models political pressure ratcheting it up over time. In ordinary fiat runs it changes outcomes very little.
Random crises only. The live app can make shocks bigger and more frequent but can’t schedule a particular crisis at a particular date, so “stormy” cases compare whole histories, not a single event.
A small sample of futures. Each case is 10 random histories of a 4,000-household economy. Directions that hold in all 10 paired runs are flagged. Smaller differences should be treated as noise.
A teaching tool, not a forecast. The simulator is a deliberately simplified economy. Treat every number here as evidence about assumptions, never as proof about the real world. Change an assumption in the app and watch the conclusion move. That is the point.
